Shocking stat of the day:

~$7.0 trillion worth of T-Bills are currently outstanding, with ~$6.1 trillion maturing within the next year.

Including the remaining maturities, ~$7.5 trillion worth of marketable Treasury debt is maturing in 2026.

Another ~$4.0 trillion matures in 2027, followed by ~$3.5 trillion in 2028.

Meanwhile, if the Fed hikes rates by 75 basis points, annual interest costs on T-bills alone could rise by ~$50 billion, equivalent to 0.15% of GDP.

This comes as much of this debt would be refinanced at higher market rates than those at which it was originally issued.

The US is set to face a massive refinancing wave at higher borrowing costs.

BREAKING: Equities now account for a record 48.2% of total US household financial assets.

This includes stocks held directly, as well as equities held indirectly through life insurance companies, private pension funds, government retirement funds, and mutual funds.

This figure has risen +13.9 percentage points since the 2022 bear market.

By comparison, at the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble peak, US households held 38.7% of their financial assets in equities.

For perspective, this proportion never exceeded 20% between 1974 and 1992.

Asset owners are winning.

BREAKING: Earnings for VLCC supertankers on the benchmark Middle East-to-China route are up to nearly $800,000 per day, an all-time high.

Rates have more than doubled over the last 2 months.

At the same time, the rate for a VLCC charter from the US Gulf to Asia is up to a record ~$29.5 million per voyage, before additional war-risk costs and fees for potential delays.

The surge has been driven by fewer vessels willing to transit the Strait of Hormuz, sharply reducing available shipping capacity.

As a result, alternative routes keep each tanker at sea for more time, further reducing the number of vessels available.

Looking ahead, earnings for VLCCs are estimated to stay above $100,000 a day into next year, more than double historical levels, which rarely exceeded $45,000 a day, according to Kpler.

Inflation is back.

Apollo's Torsten Slok says we just went through a regime change, and I agree. For 20 years a savings glut, more capital than projects, crushed interest rates. That era is over.

Now it's a savings shortage. Data centers, the power grid, and above all government deficits are all long-duration claims on a limited pool of savings. Capital finally gets to demand a higher return, and it does so at the long end of the curve.

That is why long rates are rising faster than short. The cheap-money regime that inflated every long-duration asset for two decades is structurally broken, and Washington's borrowing is first in line for the capital.

Everyone sees CPI at 3.4% and panics because it is trending upwards. Look at what's actually in the basket.

The top of the list is pure energy: fuel oil up 50%, gasoline up 27%, a supply shock from a war. The bottom is outright deflation: smartphones down 10%, used cars, appliances, and auto insurance all falling.

A few energy and service lines are dragging the average up. Strip the war-driven energy spike and there is no broad, money-driven inflation in this chart, just a supply shock sitting on top of falling goods prices. 

This is not something a rate hike fixes.

The Wall Street Journal says energy is driving inflation. Their own chart says the opposite.

Energy added over 1% to headline inflation but just 0.15% to core, the measure that strips out food and fuel. Even the projection for this quarter puts core at 0.23%. Core is running 2.4% and cooling. The pump is loud, it barely touches the trend.

Diesel hit a record $6 a gallon and crude is near $100, a supply shock from a war, not money printing. Supply shocks spike and fade. The only thing that makes inflation stick is the printing press, and no gas pump changes that.

A Sensex put option soared 4,800% in a single closing-auction window last month. A straddle that should decay to zero into expiry jumped 14% instead.

This is the world's busiest options market, and its month-old closing-auction design is so broken that the settlement itself moves prices more than the news does. Whoever can push a thin 20-minute window prints money, everyone else gets run over.

India's regulator just proposed cutting the window in half and hiding the indicative index mid-auction to stop the gaming. Until it lands, the last 20 minutes are the most dangerous trade in global equities.

Europe's diesel has never been this expensive relative to crude. The ICE gasoil crack spread just hit a record near $80 a barrel.

This is a supply story. Ukraine's strikes cut Russian diesel exports to a trickle, Houthi attacks shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, and Middle East refineries are still down from the Iran war. That is a supply shock, not inflation.

Yet the ECB and Bank of England are hiking straight into it, with UK markets now pricing 2 more increases by February. Raising rates does not un-bomb a refinery. It just chokes the economy while the actual cause sits in a war zone. Tightening into a supply shock is the oldest central-bank mistake there is.

US core CPI 'topped estimates' in August, 0.3% vs 0.2%. Cue the rate-hike panic.

The driver was a record 2.3% jump in communication prices, a one-month spike in wireless phone plans. Strip that one category and the beat vanishes. Core inflation year over year actually eased to 2.4%.

This is a phone-bill quirk, not inflation. The 500 PhD economists at the Fed are getting ready to hike off a wireless receipt, late and wrong as always. If you want the real thing, watch the money printing, not your phone bill.

Japan and the US ran a rare joint intervention to prop up the yen. It worked for exactly one move: USD/JPY fell from 164 to 154.

Morgan Stanley is already fading it. New trade: long dollar-yen, 163 target, 150 stop. They read the yen's rally as a short-term carry unwind on pension-repatriation fears they call overdone, not a real shift in fundamentals.

If they're right, the carry trade rebuilds, cheap yen funding flows back out the risk curve, and that is a tailwind for global equities. It also means the intervention bought weeks, not a trend.

US ground beef just hit a record $7.16 a pound. The cattle herd behind it is the smallest in over 50 years.

This is a supply shock, not inflation. Washington is already importing a record 20% of the beef supply and waved through 300,000 tons of cheaper Brazilian beef, and the shelf price still made a new high. You cannot import a herd back overnight.

Wholesale cattle futures sit near a one-year low while retail sets records. Only a multi-year rebuild breaks that. $7 beef is sticking around through the midterms.

Strip the scarcity out and a 177x stock compresses toward the 23x its peers trade at. That is a long way down. $TSLA

I found the arguments in the podcast very unconvincing. 

Any income generated by AI is already taxed.

If an individual uses an agent, the resulting income is taxed as individual income. If a corporation uses one, the resulting profits are taxed at the corporate level, and potentially again through dividends or capital gains.

Taxing the tool because it makes human labor less necessary is just a tax on productivity. Pretty dumb idea imo.

tweets.text:
There are so many factors here, but first and foremost, we should not be looking at this phenomena on the HODL waves (BTC denominated). As Bitcoin gets bigger, ancient, deep dormant, and lost coin continue to compress the Y-axis on supply curves, making it look smaller than it actually is.

We must look at it on the Realised Cap HODL waves (USD denominated), where several such 'spikes' in young coins become visible.

There's a tonne of additional factors including the Coldcard incident, folks moving coins to sell the LukeCashJr fork, and the time-pain capitulation that occurred between June and August. What we ended up with is 'several spikes' spread over a few months, rather than the one event usually associated with an FTX or Dec 2018 style red candle.
